item.title: EEG Resting-State Beta Band Dynamic Functional Connectivity Reveals State-Dependent Disruption of Language Network Lateralisation in First-Episode Schizophrenia.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Language disorganisation is a core feature of schizophrenia with significant functional consequences. However, its neurophysiological substrates remain poorly characterised, particularly in the early stages of the illness. This study investigated whether first-episode schizophrenia (FES) is associated with disruption in the organisation of language-network lateralisation, using both static and dynamic functional connectivity metrics in the EEG beta band. Thirty-one FES patients and 32 age-matched healthy volunteer subjects (HVS) underwent resting-state 64-channel EEG. Source-level connectivity was estimated using the weighted phase lag index with sliding windows, yielding 979 connectivity matrices per participant. Brain network states (BNS) were identified via k-means clustering. Static connectivity was obtained by time-averaging. Temporal features, graph-theoretical metrics, and language-network laterality indices were extracted for both whole-network and language-specific analyses. Group comparisons used permutation-based tests with family-wise error correction. Static connectivity yielded no significant group differences in any metric. Dynamic analysis identified six BNS. FES showed a significant increase in the variability of the temporal dynamics and graph-theory features of BNS5, a state characterised by parieto-occipital dominance. The core language network laterality index was significantly reduced in FES within BNS1, a state characterised by auditory-visual dominance. BNS1 occurrence correlated negatively with language disorganisation scores. Dynamic BNS-specific language network metrics correlated with verbal fluency performance exclusively in FES. These findings demonstrate that language dysfunction in early psychosis is expressed as state-dependent disruption of brain network stability and language lateralisation, detectable only through dynamic connectivity analysis.

item.title: A shape deformation-based framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Individualized morphological brain networks have emerged as an important framework for imaging-based connectomics. However, existing methods have focused predominantly on the cerebral cortex, leaving subcortical structures largely unexplored despite their central roles in cognition and neuropsychiatric disorders. Here, we developed a novel framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks from structural magnetic resonance imaging. Specifically, subcortical surfaces were reconstructed using a Point2Mesh-optimized multilayer perceptron architecture and vertex-wise shape deformation was quantified as the signed Euclidean distance between each vertex on an individual mesh and the corresponding vertex on the group-average template mesh. Interregional morphological connectivity in local shape deformation distributions was subsequently estimated using Jensen-Shannon Divergence. Applying this approach to the Human Connectome Project dataset, we found that subcortical morphological networks exhibited complex topological organization, including small-world architecture, modular organization, and highly connected hubs, which were consistently preserved at finer subregional scales. Analyses using an independent test-retest dataset further demonstrated fair-to-good reliability of these network properties. Importantly, these shape deformation-based networks showed significant coupling with subcortical functional networks estimated from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Leveraging large-scale multisite clinical datasets, we further demonstrated alterations of subcortical morphological networks in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder. Schizophrenia was characterized predominantly by right caudate-centered disruptions in morphological connectivity and nodal centrality, whereas major depressive disorder exhibited alterations only in nodal centrality of the right amygdala. Together, these findings establish a novel and reliable framework for investigating subcortical morphological network organization in the human brain across both healthy and psychiatric populations.

item.title: Amplitude-conditioned brain dynamics reveal widespread negative modulation and targeted positive modulation of functional networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Functional connectivity is traditionally characterized through pairwise interactions between brain regions. However, growing evidence suggests that neural communication is also shaped by higher-order interactions in which the activity of a third region modulates the coupling between others. Here, we introduce a whole-brain framework for mapping resting-state nonlinear conditional connectivity from functional MRI. For each cortical region, we quantified how spontaneous amplitude fluctuations modulate the functional connectivity of all other region pairs. This procedure generated a modulation spectrum for every connection, describing connectivity changes across multiple amplitude states of the modulator. From these spectra, we derived four interpretable features capturing modulatory strength, polarity, volatility, and nonlinear complexity. The framework was applied to resting-state data from the Human Connectome Project and evaluated using stationary surrogate models, spatial topography analyses, test-retest reliability assessments, and behavioral prediction. Surrogate analyses demonstrated that the observed modulation spectra could not be explained by static covariance structure or spectral properties alone, indicating genuine state-dependent dynamic interactions. Topographic mapping reveals a profound functional asymmetry: the macroscopic connectome is dominated by widespread negative modulatory influences, with positive modulation restricted to sparse assortative pathways. Furthermore, by evaluating the effect of temporal integration, we show that spatial and temporal aggregation robustly stabilizes these dynamic fluctuations into reliable, individual-specific traits. Finally, employing regularized predictive modeling, we demonstrate that these dynamic modulatory features can provide complementary predictive value beyond conventional static FC, particularly for capturing state-dependent affective traits such as internalizing behavior. Together, this framework unveils a structured, asymmetric, and behaviorally relevant higher-order modulatory architecture.

item.title: Subjective emotional ratings dissociate brain activation and network patterns during counterfactual outcome processing.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Human decision-making integrates outcome evaluation, counterfactual comparison, and individual traits. We investigated the neural processing of outcome-related emotions during economic decision-making by classifying feedback according to participants' subjective emotional ratings rather than objective gain-loss categories. Participants completed a Wheel of Fortune gambling task during fMRI scanning and provided emotional ratings for feedback outcomes, enabling identification of regret, relief, disappointment, and elation. We also assessed individual differences in regret proneness, maximization tendencies, alternative search, high standards, and decision difficulty. Behaviorally, emotional ratings increased with larger obtained outcomes and decreased as reference outcomes increased, indicating robust modulation of outcome evaluation by counterfactual information Whole-brain analyses revealed greater activation for low-rating than high-rating outcomes, indicating stronger neural responses to negative than positive emotions across feedback types. Complete feedback also elicited greater activation than partial feedback within the same emotional valence. Network-level analyses revealed partially dissociable neural profiles for positive and negative emotions. Positive emotions, including elation and relief, predominantly recruited the somatomotor network, whereas negative emotions, including disappointment and regret, engaged broader distributions across the default mode, dorsal attention, and other large-scale networks. Regret elicited the largest activation extent, whereas elation elicited the smallest. Region-of-interest analyses showed that bilateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) responses were significantly greater for negative than positive emotions and for complete than partial feedback conditions. Across all four emotions, right OFC activation was negatively associated with maximization. For elation, relief, and disappointment, right OFC activation was also negatively associated with alternative search and decision difficulty, whereas these associations were absent for regret. Together, these findings demonstrate that subjective emotional evaluation, counterfactual context, and decision-related traits jointly shape the neural processing of decision outcomes, while suggesting relatively trait-independent neural processing of regret.

item.title: Parietal Structural and Functional Differentiation Associated with Visual Tracking Across Motor Participation Profiles.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Purpose This study aimed to examine whether structural and resting-state functional measures of parietal subregions differ across predefined motor participation groups with comparable physical activity levels, and whether these neural measures are associated with visual tracking performance. Methods We adopted an a priori motor-cognitive grouping framework and recruited athletes accordingly, using two representative sports as operational exemplars for each profile: (1) externally driven spatial updating and action planning (ESU; basketball and taekwondo), (2) body-environment calibration and rhythmic sensorimotor integration (SCP; skating and running), and 3) internally guided control and sustained attentional precision (IPS; tai chi and shooting). A sedentary control group (CON) with low habitual physical activity was also recruited. In total, 80 college students participated. Physical activity (PA) was assessed using a standardized questionnaire. All participants underwent structural MRI and resting-state fMRI to derive gray matter volume (GMV), fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF), degree centrality (DC), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and functional connectivity (FC) within parietal subregions (S1, SPL, AG, and SMG). Supplementary SPL-based FC analyses further examined connectivity with regions of the broader visuospatial and sensorimotor network. Visual tracking was assessed using a multiple object tracking (MOT) task across three difficulty levels. Results PA levels were significantly higher in all athlete groups than in sedentary controls, with no differences among athlete groups. Across structural and resting-state functional measures, the most consistent group differences were selectively concentrated in S1 and SPL, whereas effects involving other parietal regions were less consistent across measures. Specifically, the ESU group exhibited the highest bilateral S1 GMV, the SCP group showed the highest bilateral SPL GMV, and the IPS group demonstrated the highest fALFF in both S1 and SPL. The IPS group also showed the highest ReHo in bilateral SPL. FC differed significantly across several parietal connections, with distinct connectivity patterns across the three athlete groups. MOT accuracy differed significantly across groups at all difficulty levels, with the ESU and IPS groups outperforming the SCP and CON groups overall. Across all participants, multiple S1 and SPL metrics showed modest associations with MOT performance (r = 0.20-0.40). Within athlete subgroups, stronger and task-specific associations were observed, particularly in the SCP and IPS groups (r = 0.50-0.80). Conclusions These findings identify distinct structural and functional patterns predominantly involving S1 and SPL across different motor participation profiles, despite comparable overall physical activity levels among the athlete groups. Such parietal differences are accompanied by difficulty-dependent differences in visual tracking performance and heterogeneous brain-behavior associations. Together, the results highlight S1 and SPL as the parietal regions showing the most consistent differentiation across structural and functional measures in association with distinct motor participation profiles and visual tracking performance, and provide a focused empirical basis for future investigations into the sources of this heterogeneity.

item.title: Precise modeling of task-related sensorimotor activation based on simultaneous surface electromyography.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The aim of this study was to evaluate the relationship between motor control of ankle movements and actual motor performance using simultaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and surface electromyography (EMG) in healthy individuals. Twenty participants performed dorsi-/plantarflexion of the ankle (Ankle) and gait imagery in a block design during fMRI. First-level models consisting of task regressors included either orthogonalized accelerometry (Acc) from the foot, EMG from the tibialis anterior, EMG with Acc, EMG split across conditions, or none. Each model was additionally evaluated either by default with or without a temporal derivative (TD) of the ankle movement task regressor. Voxel-wise and post-hoc region-of-interest (ROI) analyses revealed that both Acc and EMG explained fMRI signal in the primary sensorimotor cortices, while EMG was additionally associated with activation in the cerebellar vermis and the secondary somatosensory cortex. The two latter findings were, however, neither reproduced when separating the signal fluctuations during rest and gait imagery nor reflected in pairwise comparisons. Leaving out the TD reduced each model's performance by increasing unexplained variance, but resulted in more signal being explained by the EMG or Acc in the cerebellum, reflecting that it preferentially exhibited brief signal changes during transitions between conditions. Taken together, both EMG and Acc enabled capturing specific brain activity related to the movement variability; however, including the TD may significantly affect the ability to detect EMG- or Acc-related signal in regions with transient fMRI responses sensitive to changes in movement context, such as the cerebellum.

item.title: Interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention: EEG evidence for joint modulation of late perceptual processing.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Voluntary action shapes our perception through sensory predictions of its consequences. These predictions are thought to inhibit perceptual processing of predicted outcomes, leading to sensory attenuation. However, some studies have reported findings that contrast with this effect, suggesting that the influence of predictions may reflect, or interact with, attentional processes. Here, we investigated the interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention on early and late perceptual processing, with prediction and attention referring to the likelihood of a sensory event and its behavioral relevance, respectively. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded while participants viewed two sequential gratings. The orientation of the first was either predicted and self-generated or unpredicted and externally generated. Participants judged the tilt direction of the second grating relative to the first but responded only when the grating appeared in a task-relevant color. EEG analyses revealed no modulation of early visual potentials (N1a), but modulations at later processing stages. Specifically, the P3b exhibited reduced amplitude for predicted compared to unpredicted stimuli, but only when they were task-relevant, whereas task-relevance enhanced the P3b only for unpredicted stimuli. Interestingly, multivariate pattern analysis showed significant temporal clusters for decoding the grating's orientation exclusively for predicted and task-relevant stimuli, although decoding performance did not significantly differ between conditions. Furthermore, predicted and task-relevant stimuli elicited faster behavioral responses, with prediction-related P3b latency differences correlating with reaction-time differences. Overall, converging findings from the P3b, multivariate, time-frequency and behavioral analyses provide suggestive evidence that top-down attention and action-based prediction may jointly facilitate late perceptual and decision-related processing.

item.title: Stage- and context-dependent modulation of fear memory by oxytocin: Neurobiological mechanisms and implications for PTSD.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a multifactorial psychiatric condition characterized by re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and disturbances in social and emotional functioning. Within this broader clinical syndrome, persistent traumatic memories and excessive fear generalization represent important mechanistic and therapeutic domains. Despite substantial advances in understanding its neurobiological basis, current treatments remain suboptimal, with limited efficacy and high dropout rates. The neuropeptide oxytocin (OXT), a key modulator of social behavior, stress regulation, and memory, has been investigated as a potential therapeutic target. Accumulating evidence indicates that severe trauma profoundly disrupts endogenous OXTergic signaling, whereas pharmacological studies suggest that exogenous OXT can modulate fear-memory processing through region-, dose-, route-, and context-dependent mechanisms. Evidence from fear-conditioning indicates that across acquisition, consolidation, retrieval, reconsolidation, and extinction, the direction of OXT's effects is heterogeneous rather than uniformly anxiolytic and pro-extinction. OXT may influence threat discrimination, fear expression, memory updating, and extinction by modulating specific neural circuits and neurochemical pathways. However, most preclinical models capture selected dimensions of PTSD rather than the full clinical disorder. Human studies further indicate that intranasal OXT can modulate neural, physiological, and social-cognitive processes relevant to PTSD, although evidence for consistent clinical efficacy remains limited and heterogeneous. This review synthesizes current findings on OXT and its synthetic analogs within a stage- and context-dependent framework to better investigate their heterogeneous effects and assess their potential relevance and translational limitations in PTSD.

item.title: Facial emotion recognition of sadness relates to superior parietal gray matter volume in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is associated with early, regionally selective neurodegenerative changes that may affect socioemotional functioning before atrophy becomes widespread. This study examined whether structural brain alterations in MCI relate to facial emotion recognition performance. Sixty adults (30 MCI, 30 healthy controls), aged 50-86 years, completed neuropsychological testing, the Facial emotion composite Task, and structural MRI. Whole-brain voxel-based morphometry revealed no significant gray matter volume differences between groups. However, targeted region-of-interest ROI analyses demonstrated lower right amygdala and bilateral hippocampal volumes in patients with MCI. Cortical thickness analyses identified two regions with lower thickness in MCI: the right superior parietal lobule and the left posterior insula. A significant Group × Sadness interaction indicated that the association between left superior parietal gray matter volume and sadness recognition differed between groups. Follow-up analyses of the extracted values showed a positive association in MCI, although this within-group association did not reach statistical significance, and a significant inverse association in HCs. These findings suggest that early MCI involves selective thinning in association cortices supporting attention and salience processing. The sadness-specific interaction indicates that patients with MCI may rely on preserved superior parietal structure during sadness recognition, a pattern that is consistent with structural reserve accounts, although this interpretation remains speculative given the cross-sectional design.

item.title: Reward sensitivity is negatively associated with future self-continuity: the mediation role of functional connectivity between the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Reward Sensitivity refers to individual differences in the perception, evaluation, and emotional response to potential or acquired rewarding stimuli. Future self-continuity refers to the degree of psychological connection, identification, and consistency that individuals perceive between their present self and future self. Although both constructs are known to critically influence intertemporal decision-making and self-control, the shared neurobiological mechanisms linking them remain largely unexplored. To address this question, we used voxel-based morphometry and resting-state functional connectivity analyses to investigate the neural basis underlying the association between reward sensitivity and future self-continuity. Behavioral results showed reward sensitivity exhibited a significant negative correlation with future self-continuity. Moreover, voxel-based morphometry (VBM) revealed that reward sensitivity was negatively associated with gray matter volume in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC). Furthermore, resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) analysis demonstrated that the functional connectivity between the dmPFC and the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC) was positively correlated with reward sensitivity. Ultimately, mediation analysis revealed a positive indirect effect, indicating that this dmPFC-vlPFC connectivity acted as a protective neural factor in the negative relationship between reward sensitivity and future self-continuity. In conclusion, the current research offered novel insights into the impact of reward sensitivity on future self-continuity, advancing our understanding of this behavioral connection from a neurobiological perspective.

item.title: Brain imaging in dystrophinopathies.
item.description:
Journal of neurology
Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies (DMD, BMD) are caused by genetic variants in the DMD gene coding dystrophin proteins. In addition to the impairment of muscular function, these patients also present frequent cognitive and neuropsychiatric disorders due to impaired expression of several brain dystrophins: Dp427, Dp140 and Dp71. Cerebral imaging has shed new light on the impact of dystrophinopathies on brain structure, function, and connectivity. We review the brain imaging results obtained in patients and divers animal models, showing presence of mild cortical atrophy, slight modifications of structures volumes, decreased cerebral blood flood, white matter microstructure alterations, brain hypometabolism, altered connectivity, and an abnormal cerebral response to stress. We further discuss the putative progression of cerebral disorders, and their variable severity when Dp140 expression is affected in addition to that of Dp427. Some correlations between imaging parameters and cognitive and psychological impairments have been reported but remain to be confirmed.

item.title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function. Methods We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models. Results In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively). Discussion Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

item.title: Mentalizing from self and friend perspectives: Relations between inter-brain neural similarity, affective similarity and social anxiety symptoms.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Social interactions are dynamic and complex, relying on tracking variation in your own and your partner's affective and mental states. Being "in-sync" neurally and building a shared consensus can mark successful social interactions. In addition, social anxiety can impact social experiences. We used a novel, naturalistic paradigm to investigate relations between inter-brain neural similarity within mentalizing regions, affective similarity, and social anxiety symptoms. Undergraduate student friend pairs (N = 34, 85% White, 65% Women) engaged in a social interaction while videos captured from their individual perspectives were recorded. Participants watched clips of the social interaction from both their own perspective (their personal view of the social interaction) and their friend's perspective (their friend's personal view of the social interaction) while fMRI data were collected. They rated their affect after each clip. Inter-brain neural similarity was computed across three conditions: 1) Same-Stimuli: both participants viewed identical visual stimuli as in a traditional neural similarity paradigm, 2) Self-Perspective: both participants viewed the clip from their own perspective like the originally experienced social interaction, and 3) Friend-Perspective: both participants viewed the clip from their friend's perspective, a novel perspective. Participants self-reported their social anxiety symptoms, and affective similarity captured affect rating concordance within dyads. In contrast to the Same-Stimuli condition, when participants viewed the clips like they originally experienced the social interaction (Self-Perspective), greater affective similarity was associated with greater inter-brain neural similarity. When participants viewed the clips from a novel perspective (Friend-Perspective), participants lower in social anxiety symptoms exhibited greater inter-brain neural similarity with greater affective similarity; whereas participants higher in social anxiety symptoms exhibited greater inter-brain neural similarity with less affective similarity. The results suggest stimuli from socially relevant perspectives, rather than identical stimuli, may reveal more nuanced brain-behavior dynamics, allowing for a better understanding of individual differences in socioemotional experience.

item.title: Bridging language phenotypes, neural dynamics and gene regulation in autism.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) affect approximately 1% of the global population, with prevalence rising over recent decades. Although ASDs are heritable (~70%), translating genetic findings into effective therapeutics remains challenging due to the vast number of implicated risk genes (>700) and the limited influence of individual genes on disease expression. Their collective impact and convergent expression patterns of small-effect genes provide insights into ASD-related neurobiological mechanisms. Current interventions remain symptom-focused and do not address underlying neurodevelopmental mechanisms. Emerging approaches in functional genomics offer new insights into ASD pathogenesis by exploring gene expression diversity, yet clinical applications remain distant. Language deficits are among the most frequent and disabling features of ASD, profoundly affecting individuals' and families' quality of life. Recent evidence from neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies suggests disrupted neural oscillatory dynamics are linked to language deficits in ASD. Several ASD-associated genes have been implicated in biological pathways involved in the regulation of brain oscillatory dynamics, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between genetic variation, altered brain rhythms, and language impairment. We propose a neurophysiological imaging genetics framework that leverages neural oscillatory profiles as endophenotypes for targeted investigation and as functional readouts of gene expression. Within this framework, neuromodulation is proposed as an experimental approach to investigate and potentially modulate altered oscillatory dynamics associated with speech communication deficits in ASD, while integrating oscillation-related ASD candidate genes into a symptom-oriented model of functional genomics. This approach shows how integrating genetic variation, non-invasive neuroimaging, and behavioral phenotypes can advance our understanding of ASD and inform targeted, mechanism-based interventions.

item.title: Infant hippocampal and amygdala volume in an observational follow-up from a randomized clinical trial for maternal prenatal depression.
item.description:
Nature communications
Prenatal maternal depression may have intergenerational effects on offspring brain development, with potential socioemotional consequences. This observational follow-up study examines brain development and subsequent negative emotionality among 109 infants born to mothers participating in a randomized clinical trial (NCT03011801). In the prior trial, brief interpersonal psychotherapy significantly reduced prenatal depression symptoms and disorder as the published primary and secondary endpoints. Exploratory infant outcomes include hippocampal and amygdala volumes at 6 weeks and negative emotionality at 6 months. Here we show that infants of mothers randomized to interpersonal psychotherapy during pregnancy have lower right hippocampal volume than infants of mothers in the enhanced usual care group (p = .002, d = 0.62). No statistically significant group differences are observed in left hippocampal or amygdala volume. Smaller hippocampal volume predicts subsequent lower negative emotionality (r = 0.19, p = 0.045). In this study, a maternal prenatal depression intervention is associated with differences in infant brain development with implications for their subsequent emotional health.

item.title: Decoding spatial attention in the cocktail party problem using whole-head high-density fNIRS.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Spatial attention is critical for solving the cocktail party problem, a longstanding problem in neuroscience and artificial speech recognition. The ability to decode where humans are attending in a cocktail party like scene would empower applications in brain computer interfaces and assistive devices such as hearing aids. Here we demonstrate that, in an overt attention task, the attended spatial location can be decoded robustly from single trial hemodynamic responses, using a whole head high density fNIRS system. We also identify critical brain regions that make the highest contribution to decoding accuracy. Specifically, we find that decoding based on a small fraction of channels located within the left and right inferior parietal lobule (IPL) achieves maximal decoding accuracy comparable to all channels. Decoding fell close to chance in a covert auditory condition in which participants held central fixation while attending to the same talkers, indicating that auditory attention alone without orientation is not sufficient for decoding. Finally, control experiments suggest that overt-condition decoding is influenced by sustained eye position/gaze direction, not eye movement. These results support the development of fNIRS-integrated BCIs and assistive devices controlled by overt spatial attention.

item.title: Neural dynamics of auditory attention: Interactions between top-down and bottom-up processes.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Auditory attention allows listeners to navigate complex acoustic environments by prioritizing behaviorally-relevant sounds while limiting interference from competing input. This process is guided by a dynamic interplay between top-down attention, driven by behavioral goals and expectations, and bottom-up attention, triggered by stimulus-driven salience. Although this distinction remains useful at a conceptual level, growing evidence suggests that auditory attention emerges from continuous interactions between goal-directed and stimulus-driven processes that recruit partially overlapping neural systems and vary with task demands, stimulus properties, and prior experience. This review focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying attentional control and interactions between top-down and bottom-up auditory attention. It synthesizesevidence from neurophysiological, behavioral, and neuroimaging studies and explores how top-down control modulates the neural processing and attentional impact of salient input, how bottom-up signals override attentional focus, and how these interactions are shaped by task demands and individual cognitive capacity. The findings synthesized here support a view of auditory attention as a flexible and adaptive system, whose operation emerges from context-dependent interactions, with important implications for models of attention and real-world listening behaviors.

item.title: Reorienting TMS treatments for fear memories and posttraumatic stress disorder. The emerging potential of the anterior prefrontal cortex.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by re-experiencing trauma through vivid and involuntary intrusions, avoidance of cues that could trigger traumatic memories, and alterations in mood and cognition. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) offers a promising approach to modulating activity and functional coupling within neural circuits underlying these processes. To date, TMS studies in fear-conditioning research and PTSD have mainly focused on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and ventromedial (vmPFC)-connected or broader medial-prefrontal (mPFC) targets, yielding encouraging but heterogeneous effects on posttraumatic symptoms. In parallel, emerging evidence has implicated the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC; Brodmann area 10) in threat- and trauma-related processes, including memory retrieval, higher-order control of defensive responding, adaptive strategy selection, and resilience. Whereas the dlPFC and vmPFC have been incorporated into mechanistic models of fear regulation, the aPFC has received limited attention in theoretical frameworks of fear and PTSD. Here, we review TMS studies organized around dlPFC, vmPFC-connected or mPFC, and aPFC neuroanatomical targets, integrating evidence from experimental and clinical research. Based on the hierarchical model of prefrontal organization, we argue that these regions represent potential TMS targets or circuit nodes, but likely act on partially distinct mechanisms. The vmPFC appears primarily involved in early automatic downregulation of defensive responses; the dlPFC may support cognitive control strategies such as reappraisal; and the aPFC may enable a supraordinate influence over higher-order representations and avoidance-related circuitry, as well as flexible selection of emotion-regulation strategies. We conclude that integrating the aPFC into this framework may guide next-generation, mechanistically-informed TMS treatments for PTSD.
